feedback: If evidence cited is shared by both look-alikes (fins, lives in the sea), point out both animals have it: 'The shark has every one of these too — so do they decide the case?' Steer to a feature present in one group and absent in the other.
If only one reason is given, prompt: 'What is a second, independent piece of evidence you can actually SEE?'
If habitat or surface resemblance is used ('lives in water, so it's a fish'), ask 'Do other groups also live in water? So does that really prove it's a fish?'

Try the covering test: ask 'If you covered up everything except this one feature, could you still tell which group it belongs to?' If yes, it is a diagnostic feature; covering a shared feature like fins changes nothing.
When two decisive, distinguishing features are pinned, confirm the argument is complete: the claim now rests on evidence that the claimed group has and the look-alike's group lacks.
activities.intendedInsight: A scientific classification is an argument built on distinguishing evidence, not a guess from surface looks; features two look-alikes share cannot decide between them.
learnerActions: Examine an unfamiliar organism (photo or description — e.g. a pangolin or an axolotl) and collect the features it actually shows. A pangolin is covered in scales, but it has some hair on its face and underside, and the description says it feeds its young on milk, so it is a mammal. An axolotl has a backbone and external gills, but fish share both. Its four legs with toes and its moist, scaleless skin are the features that point to amphibian.
Decide which group it belongs to and file it there.
Pin at least TWO features that justify the decision — reasons, not just a placement.
Then meet a decoy pair: a dolphin beside a shark. First try to justify using 'lives in the sea, streamlined, has fins'; notice these features are shared by BOTH animals so they decide nothing.

Search for the features that actually separate them — the dolphin breathes air with lungs through a blowhole while the shark uses gills, and the dolphin feeds its young on milk while the shark does not — and use those to settle that the dolphin is a mammal and the shark is a fish.
State the full argument: claim (it's a mammal), evidence (feeds young on milk, breathes air), reasoning (only mammals do both).
activities.title: Classification detective: prove the placement

feedback: When the learner cites a decisive, non-shared feature, the challenger concedes: 'Your group has that feature and the look-alike's group does not — that settles it.'
When a shared or irrelevant feature is offered, the challenger presses: 'But the other animal has that too — try again.'
If the learner restates the group name as its own reason, ask them to name something they can actually observe.
activities.intendedInsight: A classification must survive challenge: defensible reasons cite characteristics that separate the claimed group from the alternative being compared, and you can discard a reason once you see a similar organism shares it.
learnerActions: State a classification of an organism and your supporting evidence aloud or in writing.
Respond to a taxonomist who probes each justification: 'You say mammal — what's your evidence? The shark also has fins, so why isn't the dolphin a fish?'
Drop any reason the challenger shows is shared or irrelevant, and replace it with a decisive, distinguishing characteristic.
Keep going until you can name a feature present in your claimed group and absent in the look-alike group, and explain why it settles the case.
activities.title: Defend it: taxonomist challenge dialogue

feedback: If the learner labels a shared feature as the distinguishing one, re-highlight that both animals show it.
Confirm when the learner isolates the feature present in one group and absent in the other.
activities.intendedInsight: Before constructing an argument, learners can see explicitly that some observed features are shared (non-deciding) while others are diagnostic.
learnerActions: Study an annotated comparison of two look-alikes (e.g. dolphin vs shark), where features the two share are marked one way and the features that distinguish them (e.g. lungs vs gills, feeding young on milk) are marked another.
Name, for that pair, which observed features are shared and which features separate the groups.
Explain in your own words why the shared features cannot decide the classification.
activities.title: Worked-example read: shared vs diagnostic features

feedback: For a shared-feature distractor, note that the look-alike also has it, so it cannot distinguish the groups — e.g. 'both have four legs' does not separate two four-legged animals.
For an irrelevant feature (colour, size, name), note it varies widely within groups and is not what defines membership of the group.
Confirm selections that name features present in the target group and absent in the alternative.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising which evidence is diagnostic reinforces the standard for a good classification argument; recognising a reason is not the same as independently constructing and defending one.
learnerActions: For a classified organism, select the TWO characteristics that best justify the classification (multi-select).
Match organism pairs to a feature that distinguishes their groups.
Judge whether a given reason is decisive or merely shared/irrelevant (e.g. is 'lives in the sea' good evidence that something is a fish?).
Critique a wrong justification built on a shared or irrelevant feature and say what makes it weak.
activities.title: Check: which evidence is decisive?
